evidence: Receiving DO2 online sensor: 10.24 mg/L at t=50.0h
Receiving DO2 online sensor: sharp step to 4.86 mg/L at t=50.2h, declining to 4.32 mg/L at t=52.0h (latest)
Source batches (source-1/2/3) DO2 never fell below ~7.4 mg/L at comparable times; receiving drop is anomalous
Delayed P assays (receiving): 0.99 g/L at 36h, 2.88 g/L at 48h — production on track vs source (~3 g/L at 48h)
Task constraint: minimum DO 2.0 mg/L; allowed_actions lists increase_air as [1.0, 1.15]
submission.rationale: Receiving DO2 collapsed from ~10.2 to ~4.3 mg/L between t=50 and t=52 h and continues to decline — an oxygen-demand spike unseen in any source batch. While 4.3 mg/L is still above the 2.0 mg/L minimum, the sustained downward trend threatens a constraint violation, and product (P=2.88 g/L at 48h) is actively accumulating, so stopping or cutting feed would sacrifice product mass. Increasing aeration (×1.15) directly counteracts the elevated oxygen uptake with no production penalty and restores DO margin; feed reduction is held in reserve if DO2 fails to recover. No extra assay is requested because the online DO2 sensor already establishes the abnormality and a 4h assay delay would postpone mitigation.
submission.uncertainty: The hidden cause of the DO drop (e.g., substrate pulse vs sensor fault) is unknown; if it is transient, increase_air is harmless but unnecessary, and if demand grows faster than 15% more aeration can supply, a further step (combined or strong_feed_reduction) may be needed. DO2 trajectory after intervention cannot be predicted exactly; the ~-0.2 mg/L/h decline rate extrapolated from 50.2-52.0 h could reach ~2 mg/L in roughly 10 h if unaddressed, though this extrapolation is uncertain (only ~2 h of post-drop data).
